summary.text: Nuclear fusion is a reaction in which two or more atomic nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus.
The difference in mass between what goes in and what comes out shows up as released or absorbed energy, and active stellar cores are powered by fusion.
Fusion typically needs very high temperature, density and confinement time, and fusion power research seeks to use it for energy.

facts.label: Where energy comes from
facts.value: The difference in nuclear binding energy before and after

facts.label: Elements it makes
facts.value: All elements lighter than nickel, in the Big Bang and in stars

facts.label: First experiment
facts.value: Widely held to be a 1934 deuterium experiment at Cavendish

items.prompt: In 1919 a new instrument showed that four hydrogen atoms weigh more than one helium atom. What did Eddington predict from that in 1920?

options.label: Stars gain their light from burning chemical fuel
Stars have to be much heavier than first thought
Stars could be powered by turning lighter atoms into the heavier one
Stars must slowly lose helium into space

items.explain: Eddington correctly predicted that fusion of hydrogen into helium could be the primary source of stellar energy.

items.prompt: Two very light nuclei fuse into a heavier nucleus that is still lighter than nickel-62. What happens to energy?

options.label: Energy is released
Energy is absorbed
No energy changes hands
Energy is released only if the nuclei are heavy

items.explain: Fusion that produces nuclei lighter than nickel-62 is exothermic, because of the positive gradient of the nuclear binding energy curve.

items.prompt: A researcher wants nuclei that fuse most readily for energy. Which should they choose?

options.label: Very heavy nuclei, the actinides
Nickel-62 nuclei
Any nuclei, since all fuse equally well
Some of the lightest, such as deuterium and tritium

items.explain: The most fusible nuclei are among the lightest, while the opposite process, fission, is most energetic for very heavy nuclei such as the actinides.

items.prompt: Hans Bethe worked out how stars turn hydrogen into helium. Which process dominates in a Sun-type star?

options.label: The CNO cycle
The proton–proton chain
The deuterium–tritium reaction
Fission of heavy nuclei

items.explain: Bethe and Critchfield enumerated the proton–proton chain that dominates Sun-type stars, while the CNO cycle is common to higher-mass stars.

items.prompt: Theory assumed the deuterium–tritium reaction would be about as likely as deuterium–deuterium. What did Bretscher find in 1946?

options.label: It was far less likely, about 100 times smaller
It was exactly as likely as theory said
A resonance made its cross-section about 100 times larger
It could not happen at all

items.explain: Bretscher discovered a resonance enhancement giving the deuterium–tritium reaction a cross-section about 100 times larger.

items.prompt: Where did the elements lighter than nickel come from?

options.label: Fusion, in the Big Bang and in stars
Fission of only the heaviest nuclei
Chemical reactions deep inside planets
Fusion devices built by people

items.explain: Nucleosynthesis via fusion, in the Big Bang and in stars, creates all elements lighter than nickel.
